Cut long and heavy, the Wayfarer Long Cloak is made for arrivals in bad weather. A brushed wool blend with a water-resistant finish falls from the shoulders like a curtain, the deep hood shadows the face, and a hidden inner pocket keeps a star chart dry. It comes in desert sand and storm grey, sized from S to XXL, with enough room to wear over armour or an everyday coat. It smells faintly of woodsmoke after the first trip, and that is how you know it is working.

Soft, breathable and quietly ceremonial, the Initiate Training Robe is what students of the Strand wear on their first day and long after. Three layers of washed cotton gauze wrap across the body and close with a simple tie belt, leaving the arms free for drills. It comes in one unbleached oat colour, because tradition says an initiate earns their colour later. Light enough for summer, layered enough for a cold hangar, it softens with every wash. Cold water, line dry, and it will last for years.

The Drift Boot Wraps turn any pair of boots into crew issue. Waxed canvas wraps the ankle and shin, buckled with leather straps and small cast-brass fittings, and adjusts to almost any boot or trainer. On a metal deck they soften every step; on a costume they finish the whole silhouette. Deckhands give a pair to every new member of the crew, and the canvas creases into its owner's walk within a week. Simple, affordable and the easiest way to look like you have travelled far.

Felt slippers for cold stone floors and long meditations about whether you locked the speeder.
Loose-weave scarf in two sand tones. Covers the face from dust storms and from acquaintances.

Forged for the long nights between stations, the Vanta Arc Trainer is the blade most travellers carry first and keep longest. Its hilt is milled from a single bar of aluminium, bead-blasted to a soft graphite grey and wrapped in numbered leather. Wake it and the polycarbonate blade fills with a slow, even glow in any of twelve colours, from comet white to deep ember. It is balanced for drills and light sparring, quiet on the belt, and loud in a dark room. Built to arrive whole, packed in a moulded sleeve, and to outlast the hands that train with it.

Every blade starts with a hilt, and the Strand Emitter is the one built to be changed, carried and remembered. Machined aluminium, anodised in four station finishes, with a threaded end cap that comes away to reveal a small keepsake slot. It fits every blade we make, so a single core can wear a new face for each journey. The grip ridges are cut by hand on the final pass, which is why each hilt feels faintly different in the palm. Light, honest, and built to take a scuff and keep its shine.

The Sovereign Arc Duellist is the piece the rest of the armoury is measured against. Its hilt pairs warm brass with blackened steel, finished by hand in a run of forty per cycle. A duel-rated blade carries a smooth-swing sound core that answers every movement with a low, rising tone, and the ignition flickers like a distant star caught mid-collapse. Twenty-four colours, a numbered certificate and a fitted display case come with it. This is not a first blade. It is the one you hand down.

A two-ended trainer for people who find one end insufficient. Twice the blade, twice the apologies to the lampshade.
A thumb-sized hilt that lights a 4 cm blade. Finds keys, impresses nobody over nine, sells out every winter.
Five metres of textured grip tape. For hilts, racquets and the one drawer handle that keeps coming off.

Does not ignite. Does not need to. Sits on a wall and makes guests lower their voices.

A blade is only light around a heart, and the Ember Core Reliquary is where that heart rests. Turned from fallen walnut and closed with a brass hinge and quiet magnetic latch, it cradles a single resin core crystal on deep velvet. Hold the crystal up to a lamp and it throws a slow amber fire across the wall. The case sits on a shelf like an heirloom and travels like a tool, small enough for a coat pocket and sturdy enough for a long haul. Care is simple: a dry cloth, no solvents.

When a blade crosses a galaxy it travels in the Drift Vault. A machined aluminium shell, twin combination locks and a pressure valve keep the outside world outside, while precision-cut foam holds blade, hilt and core in their own places. It rolls quietly on sealed wheels, lifts by a padded handle, and opens with a soft exhale as the valve equalises. A serial number is etched inside the lid and logged on dispatch, so every vault can be traced from our dock to yours. Expensive, deliberate, and built to arrive.

The Orbit Display Stand gives a blade a place to rest that feels earned. A heavy cast-iron base, powder-coated in graphite, holds two felt-lined cradles that adjust to any of our blades or hilts. Its lines follow the docking clamps of the old Strand ring, so a blade on the stand looks less like a toy on a shelf and more like a ship in berth. Weighted to stay level on a bookcase, a desk or a moving deck, it turns a corner of the room into a quiet hangar. Assembly takes one minute and no tools.
Lint-free cloth for crystals, lenses and the screen you keep touching. Three in a pack because you will lose two.
Send a cracked core back in this padded pouch and get store credit. Honest about failure, which is rare in cores.
A pocket tin for two cores. Rattles pleasantly. Confuses airport scanners in a way that is legal but memorable.
Forty slots, a hygrometer and a lock. For collectors who have stopped pretending it is a phase.

The Quartermaster Utility Belt is built like the ones worn by those who keep a ship running. Full-grain leather, hand-stitched with waxed thread, carries six detachable pouches and a blade clip that angles for either draw. Brass hardware ages into a warm patina, and every pouch can move, so the belt grows with what you carry. It holds a hilt, a core reliquary, a star chart and a ration bar without a rattle. Heavy in the hand, light on the hips, and made to be repaired rather than replaced.

The Ranger Hilt Holster holds a hilt the way a scabbard holds a sword: close, steady and ready. Leather is moulded over a rigid core around a real hilt, so the fit is exact and the draw is clean. It rides on a belt up to six centimetres wide or drops to the thigh with the included strap, as the outer-station rangers wear it. A retention snap closes with a crisp click. It is balanced for an effortless draw on the move, and built to sit on your belt for a decade.

The Pilgrim Field Pack is cut for walking a long way with little. Twenty-two litres of waxed canvas sit on a stamped leather base, close with a roll-top and brass buckle, and ride on padded straps that stay comfortable through a full day. A side sleeve takes a blade up to ninety centimetres, so your arc travels with you and not in the hold. Weather beads off the canvas, and the leather darkens into the road. Currently out of stock, with the next run in the making.
